claims.text: A machine-learning-guided, multi-step thermomechanical workflow will produce a refined microstructure in advanced metallic alloys.
The machine-learning-guided workflow will substantially increase strength without compromising ductility.
Multi-principal-element or refractory alloys generally have moderate strength and limited ductility after conventional processing.
Machine learning can correlate processing temperatures, times, and strain rates with resulting microstructural features.
Those learned correlations can guide selection of thermomechanical parameters that enhance strength-ductility synergy.
A design-of-experiments campaign combining varied working and heat-treatment schedules, tensile tests, and microscopy can train and validate the proposed model.
Nanoscale precipitates can serve as the structural mediator of simultaneous strength and ductility improvements.
Stable lamellar phases can serve as the structural mediator of simultaneous strength and ductility improvements.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates facilitate dislocation transmission or slip and relieve stress concentrations that otherwise promote premature cracking.
The proposed precipitates or lamellar phases obstruct dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
Machine learning identifies complex relationships among process conditions, precipitation behavior, and dislocation activity.
The tuned microstructure enhances strain hardening.
Relieving stress concentrations and preventing early crack initiation can preserve ductility while attaining high strength.
The processed alloys will exhibit yield strength above 2 GPa.
The processed alloys will retain tensile ductility above 10%.
Simple cold working or single-step heat treatment typically raises strength at the cost of severe ductility loss.
The workflow requires a sufficiently large and representative dataset to capture processing-structure-property relationships.
Limited data, incomplete process ranges, or overfitting can reduce model accuracy and transferability.
The magnitude of improvement depends on alloy composition, data coverage, and machine-learning model fidelity.
Failure of the ML-guided samples to show higher yield strength together with comparable or improved ductility relative to controls would falsify the hypothesis.
